segments.text: What's up guys, welcome back to CrimeTimeSnacks.
Before he was a household name, Scott Peterson was a college athlete with a problem.
He was kicked off the Arizona State golf team after taking a visiting high school recruit out drinking.
It is a small detail from his early years, but it shows a crack in the perfect image he liked to project.
To understand how this case captivated the country, we have to look at where it started.
Scott Lee Peterson was born on October 24, 1972, down in San Diego.
His father, Lee, owned a crate-packaging company, and his mother, Jackie, ran a boutique in La Jolla called The Put On.
They had six kids from previous relationships, but Scott was their only child together.
He grew up sharing a bedroom with his half-brother John in the family's two-bedroom apartment.
He picked up golf early and showed real talent.
By age 14, he could already beat his dad on the course.
He wanted to go pro and even played on the same high school team as future legend Phil Mickelson, eventually becoming one of the top junior golfers in San Diego.
In 1990, Scott took a partial golf scholarship to Arizona State University, where Mickelson was also enrolled.
His father later testified that the heavy competition there discouraged him.
That is when the drinking incident happened.
The father of a young recruit named Chris Couch found out Scott took his son drinking on a recruiting trip, complained to the coach, and Scott lost his spot on the roster.
Scott transferred to Cuesta College and eventually landed at California Polytechnic State University.
He shifted his focus to agricultural business, graduating in 1998.
His professors considered him a model student, with one even saying he wouldn't mind having a class full of Scott Petersons.
He presented the image of a well-mannered, hardworking guy.
While Scott was navigating his college years, his future wife was growing up a few hours north.
Laci Denise Rocha was born in May 1975 in Escalon, California, to Dennis and Sharon Rocha.
She was raised in Modesto and attended Grace M. Davis High School.
By all accounts, Laci was vivacious, warm, and deeply adored by her family and friends.
Laci and Scott met in 1994 when they were both students at Cal Poly.
They seemed like a great match and got married in August 1997.
After graduation, they settled into building a life together, eventually moving back to Laci's hometown of Modesto.
To the outside world, they were the all-American couple.
Let's unpack that golf scholarship at Arizona State.
But the case file gives us a little more context on what he was facing before the drinking incident.
They both ended up at ASU in 1990.
The dynamic in college was completely different, though.
He wasn't just up against Mickelson.
The team also featured another unnamed future professional golfer.
Scott was a top junior player, but the reality of that roster was heavy.
After he transferred to Cal Poly, he had to figure out a new path.
He didn't jump straight into agricultural business.
The record shows he initially planned to major in international business before making the switch.
That pivot seemed to work out for him.
He earned his agribusiness degree in 1998.
That is when he took classes with professor Jim Ahern, the man who called him a model student.
Fast forward a few years.
By the winter of 2002, Scott and Laci were expecting their first child.
Laci was eight months pregnant with a boy they planned to name Conner Lee Peterson.
Her due date was in February 2003.
But everything changed on the morning of Christmas Eve.
That is the day Laci vanished from their home.
Scott told police that everything seemed fine when he left the house that morning.
He told multiple people he was heading out to play golf.
He also mentioned that Laci was planning to walk their Golden Retriever, McKenzie, around the same time.
But the timeline shifted.
By Scott's own account, he decided it was too cold for the golf course.
He changed his plans and decided to go fishing instead.
To do that, he went to a warehouse at his place of employment.
He picked up a fourteen-foot aluminum boat.
Interestingly, his own family later said they had no idea he even owned this boat.
He then drove roughly ninety miles away from Modesto to the Berkeley Marina on the San Francisco Bay.
He told investigators he spent about two hours out on the water.
When he finally returned home, he noticed Laci's car was still parked in the driveway.
Laci was nowhere to be found.
The case file shows that Scott then washed his clothes and took a shower.
At 5:17 p.m., he picked up the phone and called Laci's mother, Sharon.
He asked if Laci was over there.
She wasn't.
Sharon suggested he start calling Laci's friends to check on her.
She also found it highly peculiar that Scott was already saying Laci was missing.
After making several rounds of phone calls, the family went into complete panic mode.
It was Sharon's partner, Ron Gratski, who ultimately dialed 911.
You know how the timeline ended with that frantic 911 call on Christmas Eve.
But let's look at how this relationship actually started.
Scott got a job working at a restaurant in Morro Bay.
It was a spot called the Pacific Café.
Laci used to drop by the restaurant every now and then.
She wasn't going there to see Scott at first.
She was just visiting a friend of hers who also worked on the staff.
That is where they first crossed paths.
In the middle of 1994, Laci made the first move.
She sent Scott her phone number.
It was a bold step, but she was entirely sure of what she wanted.
The record shows she even told her mother that she had just met the man she was going to marry.
Scott made the call.
They started dating, and things moved fast.
As the relationship got more serious, Scott made a major life decision.
You remember his background on the golf course.
He finally put aside his dreams of playing professional golf.
He decided to focus entirely on a business career so they could build a life together.
They dated for two years before officially moving in together.
When they finally tied the knot, they did it at the Sycamore Mineral Springs Resort.
While Scott was finishing up his senior year, Laci took a job in a nearby town called Prunedale.
It looked like the perfect foundation for a young couple.
But the case file points to an early crack in that foundation.
Prosecutors later stated that it was around this exact time that Scott engaged in his first extramarital affair.
They never revealed the specific details or the identity of the person involved.
It is just a stark fact sitting in the trial record.
To the outside world, though, everything was moving according to plan.
After Scott graduated, they went into business for themselves.
They opened a sports bar down in San Luis Obispo called The Shack.
They ran that bar for a few years before deciding it was time to start a family.
They put The Shack up for sale and finalized the deal in April 2001.
By October 2000, they had already purchased a three-bedroom, two-bath bungalow on Covena Avenue.
It cost them a hundred and seventy-seven thousand dollars.
It sat in an upscale neighborhood near East La Loma Park.
Laci took a part-time job working as a substitute teacher.
Her family says she devoted her energy to being the perfect housewife, cooking, entertaining, and watching Martha Stewart.
Scott landed a solid corporate job to support them.
He was hired by Tradecorp U.S.A., a new subsidiary of a European fertilizer company.
The job paid him five thousand dollars a month before taxes.
They had the house, the steady income, and a baby on the way.
It was the exact life they had planned out back in Morro Bay.
You just heard the timeline of how they built their early life together.
The 1997 wedding at Sycamore Mineral Springs.
On paper, it looked like the American dream.
But I want you to focus on that first extramarital affair.
Prosecutors put it right there in the record.
It happened right around the time Laci was working in Prunedale and Scott was finishing his Bachelor of Science degree in June 1998.
The state never named the woman.
They never gave us the specifics of the relationship.
It is just a documented fact that Scott stepped out on his marriage almost immediately after it started.
By the time they sold the sports bar in April 2001 to move to Modesto, they were projecting total stability.
Laci was getting ready to be a mother.
Her younger sister later noted how much energy Laci put into being the perfect housewife.
But that early affair established a pattern.
It was a pattern that would surface again in a massive way just a few years later.
In November 2002, a friend introduced Scott to a massage therapist from Fresno named Amber Frey.
What the evidence actually shows is that they met on November 20.
Scott told her he was a single man.
They started a romantic relationship right then and there.
A few weeks later, on December 9, he changed his story.
He told Amber he was actually a widower.
He said this upcoming Christmas would be his first one without his wife.
Keep in mind, Laci was alive and well at home.
She was eight months pregnant with Conner.
But Scott was already telling people he had lost her.
Detectives eventually looked hard at those dates.
Based on the timeline Amber provided, investigators believed Scott began planning the murder two weeks before Laci actually disappeared.
Amber went to the police on December 30.
That is when she told them everything Scott had said about being a widower.
Investigators realized they had an opportunity.
They gave Amber a recording device.
They asked her to tape her phone calls with Scott, hoping he would confess or let something slip.
The case file shows she eventually recorded dozens of conversations.
While Amber was recording those calls, the police made a move.
On January 15, 2003, they sat down with Laci's immediate family.
They told them about Amber Frey.
The record shows that the moment Sharon Rocha learned about the affair, she told detectives she believed Scott killed her daughter.
The family reached a breaking point.
On January 24, Laci's brother Brent held a press conference.
He announced that Scott had called him on January 16 to admit the affair.
Brent told the public the family was withdrawing their support for Scott.
They cited his lack of communication and cooperation.
Later that exact same day, Amber Frey stepped in front of the cameras to explain her own role in the investigation.
There was one more financial detail investigators uncovered.
Scott had taken out a two hundred fifty thousand dollar life insurance policy on Laci.
It was another documented piece of the puzzle sitting right there in the file.
The case file shows they made that decision specifically to relocate to Modesto.
It was Laci's hometown, and they were ready to start a family.
The move required a complete career shift for Scott.
He traded the life of an independent business owner for a strict corporate structure.
He took that position with Tradecorp U.S.A. to guarantee a steady paycheck.
It gave him a reliable salary, and the agricultural focus fit perfectly with his college degree.
Laci supplemented that income with her substitute teaching shifts.
Let's look at the timeline of that transition.
They closed the deal on the bar in the spring, but they had already purchased the Modesto house months earlier.
It shows they were planning this next phase carefully.
It was a very different daily routine from standing behind the counter at The Shack.
To the outside observer, the Modesto move was a total success.
They transitioned from college students to bar owners to suburban professionals in just a few years.
The foundation for their family was completely set.
But that foundation would eventually become the exact thing prosecutors said he wanted to escape.
When the trial began on June 1, 2004, the state laid out their theory of the motive.
They argued that Scott wanted to be completely free from married life.
They told the jury he wanted to avoid the financial and personal obligations of parenthood to pursue his relationship with Amber.
Because of the massive local publicity, that trial had to be moved out of Stanislaus County.
They held the proceedings in Redwood City over in San Mateo County.
Scott was represented by defense attorney Mark Geragos.
He faced two felony counts of murder with premeditation and special circumstances, making him eligible for the death penalty.
He pleaded not guilty at his arraignment on April 21, 2003.
That arraignment happened just days after a grim discovery on the eastern shore of the San Francisco Bay.
On April 13, people walking near Point Isabel Regional Shoreline found the body of a male infant.
The very next day, a human female torso was discovered about a mile away on that same shoreline.
By April 18, the California Attorney General confirmed it was Laci and Conner.
The medical examiner noted Laci's body was missing her head, neck, and lower limbs, which was consistent with prolonged submersion in the water.
The autopsy showed Conner was a full-term, viable fetus who had not taken a single breath after birth.
Laci's manner of death was ruled a homicide, and the cause of Conner's death was recorded as the homicide of his mother.
The record shows they washed ashore less than two miles from where Scott claimed he was fishing.
On the exact same day those bodies were identified, police arrested Scott at a golf course down in San Diego.
He had recently bleached his hair and changed the color of his car.
When investigators searched his vehicle, they found a large amount of cash, his brother's ID card, camping equipment, and multiple cell phones.
He was actually on the phone with Amber Frey when the officers walked up to him.
On paper, it looked like the American dream.
Prosecutors put it right there in the record.
The state never named the woman.
They never gave us the specifics of the relationship.
Laci was getting ready to be a mother.
She loved cooking and entertaining.
She was known to watch Martha Stewart.
Then, in 2002, Laci discovered she was pregnant.
She was due on February 10, 2003.
To the outside world, the Petersons were living the exact life they had planned.
Let's look closely at the day before she vanished.
On December 23, at 5:45 p.m., Laci and Scott went to a place called Salon Salon.
That is where Laci's sister, Amy Rocha, worked.
Amy cut Scott's hair, just like she did every month.
While he was in the chair, Scott made an offer.
Amy had ordered a fruit basket from a nearby retailer.
Scott told her he would pick it up for her the next day.
He said he was going to be playing golf at a course right by that shop.
Later that evening, around 8:30 p.m., Sharon Rocha spoke with her daughter on the phone.
The case file shows that Amy, Sharon, and Scott were the last three people known to have spoken to Laci.
The next morning is when the accounts fracture.
Scott told police he last saw his wife at about 9:30 a.m. He claimed Laci was watching a Martha Stewart television episode about meringue.
He said her plan for the day was to mop the floor, bake cookies, and take that dog walk we talked about earlier.
The timeline of that dog being found is heavily disputed.
A neighbor named Karen Servas said she found McKenzie wandering alone.
She put the dog back in the Petersons' yard.
Another neighbor, Mike Chiavetta, said he saw the dog at about 10:45 a.m. while he was outside playing catch.
Meanwhile, a local paper reported that an unnamed female neighbor found the dog with a muddy leash and returned him to the yard.
The accounts simply do not match up.
While the neighborhood was finding the dog, Scott was out of town.
At 2:15 p.m., he left a voicemail on Laci's phone.
He said, 'Hey, Beautiful.
I'm leaving Berkeley.'
He also told police that when he got home, he was the one who found McKenzie in the backyard.
He claimed he relayed this detail to Sharon, but she explicitly denied that account in her own book.
There is another glaring inconsistency in the record.
When friends and relatives started gathering at the house that evening to look for Laci, multiple people testified that Scott told them he had been golfing all day.
A neighbor and his wife also overheard Scott saying he had been golfing.
That directly contradicted his own story to police about changing his plans.
We have already touched on the pregnancy.
By December 2002, Laci was eight months along.
They had chosen the name Conner for their son.
The case file shows they were actively preparing for a February 2003 due date.
From the outside looking in, they projected the absolute picture of a happy, growing family.
They were young, established in Modesto, and just weeks away from becoming parents.
But as we just unpacked, that outward appearance did not match the facts.
The image of the perfect expectant father was quietly fracturing behind closed doors.
Let's look at how that fracture spilled into public view while Laci was still missing.
The record shows Scott's behavior during the search raised massive red flags.
At one point, he spoke to a reporter about a potential sighting of Laci up in Longview, Washington.
He even told his mother that he had discussed this tip with the authorities in Longview.
But investigators later found out he never actually made that call.
The disconnect kept growing.
When police held a news conference to announce they were officially investigating Laci's disappearance as a homicide, Laci's family was right there in attendance.
Scott did not show up.
The media attention on this case exploded.
It evoked a national reaction that people compared to the O.J.
Simpson case.
It got so intense that Judge Al Girolami banned news cameras from the courtroom at the preliminary hearing.
He also issued a strict gag order on the attorneys and participants to try and preserve Scott's right to a fair trial.
When the trial was moved to San Mateo County, the new judge, Alfred Delucchi, also banned cameras.
The frenzy was so big that USA Network aired a made-for-TV movie called The Perfect Husband: The Laci Peterson Story, starring Dean Cain, in 2004, the same year the jury reached its verdict.
Behind the scenes, the financial battle was just as intense.
Laci's family filed a lawsuit to stop Scott from making money off his story.
In February 2004, a judge ruled that Scott could actually profit from it.
In response, Laci's mother, Sharon Rocha, filed a wrongful death lawsuit for over five million dollars.
By April 2005, she upped that ask to twenty-five million dollars.
Eventually, a judge ruled that the proceeds from that life insurance policy would go directly to Sharon.
Four years later, she dropped the lawsuits.
When the trial finally happened, circumstantial evidence was king.
The court seated a twelve-person jury with six alternates.
But the pressure in that room was immense.
Two jurors were thrown out for misconduct.
A third juror left because of intense arguments inside the jury room.
Despite the chaos, they reached a decision.
Scott was convicted of first-degree murder for Laci and second-degree murder for Conner.
The crowd gathered outside the courthouse was so loud that their cheers actually reached the courtroom.
The jury unanimously recommended death, and the judge sent him to California's death row at San Quentin State Prison.
But the legal fight did not end there.
In 2020, Scott's death sentence was overturned.
In 2021, he was re-sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
By 2022, he was transferred to Mule Creek State Prison.
Today, he continues to maintain his innocence.
The Los Angeles Innocence Project has recently taken up his claim, arguing that new evidence creates reasonable doubt.
And the media is still watching.
On August 20, 2024, a documentary series called Face to Face with Scott Peterson premiered on Peacock, featuring his first on-camera interview in decades.
You already know about that introduction in November 2002.
You also know they started a romantic relationship right after that meeting on November 20.
But the case file holds more details about what actually happened between them.
When Scott initiated that relationship, he did not just lie about being a single man.
Amber later testified in court that he also lied to her about where he lived.
He built a completely false reality.
When the news of Laci's disappearance finally broke publicly, that illusion shattered.
Amber saw the media coverage.
She realized the man she was dating was at the center of a massive missing persons investigation.
That is what prompted her to contact the police.
We discussed how she agreed to work with investigators and record their phone calls.
But the content of those dozens of recordings is what really matters.
The tapes capture Scott telling elaborate, demonstrably false stories.
He lied repeatedly about his whereabouts.
He lied about his daily circumstances.
He was weaving these fictions on the phone while search parties were out looking for his pregnant wife.
When the trial eventually started, prosecutors made those recordings a centerpiece of their case.
They played the audio directly for the jury.
The state used his own voice to show a clear pattern of deception.
Those tapes proved deeply damaging to his credibility.
They showed a man who was entirely comfortable maintaining multiple lies at the exact same time.
The state built their case on more than just those phone calls.
Prosecutors presented evidence showing Scott had purchased that aluminum fishing boat shortly before the murder.
They also showed the court that he had specifically researched the tides and currents of the San Francisco Bay.
We know he was ultimately arrested in San Diego.
The arrest report shows he was carrying nearly fifteen thousand dollars in cash.
He had also bleached his goatee to match his hair.
After they took him into custody, he was held without bail pending the capital murder charges.
In court, the medical details were difficult to hear.
The coroner testified that the official cause of death for Laci could not be definitively established.
Her remains were in an advanced state of decomposition.
The autopsy also confirmed a tragic detail about Conner.
The medical examiner determined the infant died in utero, or immediately after being expelled from Laci's body when it decomposed in the water.
It was a heavy burden for the courtroom.
The jury was made up of six men and six women.
They had to weigh all of this circumstantial evidence, from the tidal research to the cash.
They finally delivered their verdict twenty-three months after Laci first vanished.
We unpacked how the neighbors found the dog wandering the street.
But the case file holds one more crucial detail about the night before Laci vanished.
A neighbor told investigators they saw Scott outside the house loading a large object wrapped in tarps into his truck.
The next afternoon, the panic set in quickly.
When Scott returned from the Berkeley Marina and finished washing his clothes, he started checking the street.
One of his neighbors later said Scott knocked on his door to ask if he had seen Laci.
We know he called Laci's mother at 5:17 p.m. The family did not hesitate to get the authorities involved.
Scott and Laci's stepfather both officially reported her missing.
The police log shows the department received that report shortly before 6 p.m. It was the beginning of a massive search effort.
Detectives immediately scrutinized Scott's fishing trip.
They considered his alibi highly unusual for that time of year.
The record notes that most experienced fishermen do not choose a cold winter holiday to fish entirely alone in the San Francisco Bay.
They also looked closely at the boat itself.
We know he pulled it from a warehouse at his workplace.
The prosecution argued Laci had never seen the boat while alive.
The defense pushed back on that.
A witness testified they saw Laci at the warehouse with the boat the day before she vanished.
As the sun went down on Christmas Eve, the situation at the house escalated.
Friends and family began gathering at the Peterson home to help look for Laci.
That is when Scott's story started to fracture in real time.
A relative of Laci's later testified about a specific conversation that night.
While everyone was frantically searching, Scott told this relative that he had been out playing golf earlier in the day.
He was telling the police one thing and his family another.
Now he was repeating that exact same story inside the house.
Investigators also focused on the physical evidence back at the house.
You remember that McKenzie was found with his leash still attached.
For the police, that specific detail pointed to a grim theory.
They believed it suggested Laci might never have left the house for her walk at all.
The sheer scale of the disappearance became impossible to ignore.
A young woman who was seven-and-a-half months pregnant vanishing on a holiday morning set off alarm bells everywhere.
The story immediately attracted nationwide media interest.
It was the start of a media frenzy that would define the case for decades.
When the Modesto Police Department got that call, they moved fast.
Detectives Allen Brocchini and Jon Buehler responded to the house on Covena Avenue.
They took one look at the situation and immediately became the lead investigators.
The case file shows exactly what they found inside.
The detectives located Laci's personal belongings right there in the house.
Her keys, wallet, sunglasses, and purse were all sitting in a closet.
Detective Brocchini later told the press that leaving without contacting her family was completely out of character for Laci.
The initial search effort focused heavily on the immediate Modesto area.
Over thirty police officers and firefighters deployed on foot, horseback, and bicycles.
They brought in canine units and used searchlight-equipped helicopters to scan Dry Creek and the surrounding neighborhoods.
They even put watercraft in the local channels to look for any sign of her.
The community response was absolutely staggering.
The very next day, more than nine hundred of Laci's family members, friends, and neighbors hit the streets to post missing-person flyers.
They needed a place to organize everyone, so they set up a dedicated command center at the local Red Lion Hotel.
That space became the central hub for taking phone calls, recording new developments, and circulating information to the search parties.
Volunteers handed out posters and tied blue and yellow ribbons all around the city.
The husband of one of Laci's friends even launched the original version of a website called LaciPeterson.com to get the word out globally.
Eventually, over fifteen hundred volunteers were working at the command center, distributing flyers, and holding candlelight vigils.
While the volunteers searched Modesto, the two lead detectives were quietly evaluating the husband.
Almost immediately, Brocchini and Buehler suspected foul play.
Buehler later said he was thrown off by Scott's calm, cool demeanor during those crucial early hours.
He noted a complete lack of questioning from Scott about what the police were doing to find his wife.
Buehler described Scott's behavior as a strange combination of polite and arrogant.
The detective felt Scott was disaffectedly distant, rather than acting like a man crushed by his pregnant wife's disappearance.
But at that early stage of the investigation, Laci's family was not ready to point fingers.
The Rocha family publicly defended Scott, telling everyone they were the ideal couple.
For nearly four months, that massive command center in Modesto kept the search alive.
The volunteers kept handing out flyers, and the reward money sat untouched.
But the local search effort eventually ran out of ground to cover.
As winter turned to spring, the focus shifted entirely away from the Central Valley.
The breakthrough did not come from a dedicated search party or a police helicopter.
It came completely by chance.
When that male infant was found on April 13, the entire trajectory of the case shifted to the San Francisco Bay.
That discovery cemented it.
The authorities were no longer just looking for a missing person.
Once those remains were found roughly a mile apart, the local investigation became a state-wide reality.
The state took over the formal identification process.
The case file shows California Attorney General Bill Lockyer handled the official announcement.
On April 18, he confirmed the devastating truth to a waiting public.
The bodies belonged to Laci and Conner.
That identification set off an immediate chain reaction.
He was taken into custody while holding a cell phone, still talking to Amber Frey.
The months of desperate searching were officially over.
The double homicide investigation had begun.

You already know the jury handed down that guilty verdict in 2004.
But the fight over that sentence took over a decade to play out.
Let's look at exactly how the legal record shifted.
In July 2012, his defense team filed an automatic appeal.
His attorney, Cliff Gardner, submitted a four-hundred-and-twenty-three-page brief to the Supreme Court of California.
They argued that massive pre-trial publicity and incorrect evidentiary rulings deprived him of a fair trial.
They also attacked the reliability of the scent-tracking dogs used at the Berkeley Marina.
The state fought back.
The Attorney General's office filed their response, arguing the jury was fair and impartial.
The two sides traded briefs for years.
It took until June 2020 for the California Supreme Court to actually hear the arguments.
The defense hammered on jury selection.
They pointed out that almost half of the prospective jurors admitted in questionnaires that they thought he was guilty before the trial even started.
But the biggest issue came down to the death penalty itself.
The defense argued the trial judge made a critical mistake when dismissing potential jurors.
On August 24, 2020, the court handed down a unanimous seven-to-zero decision.
They upheld the double murder convictions.
But they completely overturned the death sentence.
Justice Leondra Kruger wrote the explanation.
She stated that the trial judge improperly dismissed jurors who simply opposed capital punishment.
The judge failed to ask if those individuals could put their personal views aside to follow the law.
Because of that specific error, the death penalty was off the table.
At first, prosecutors announced they were going to retry the penalty phase.
They wanted to put him back on death row.
But by June 2021, they reversed that decision entirely.
That brought the case to Judge Anne-Christine Massullo.
On December 8, 2021, she officially re-sentenced him.
He also received a concurrent sentence of fifteen years to life.
After that, he was permanently moved off death row.
The appeals process is still moving.
But the convictions themselves remain intact.
